▶ 0:16
010:00–1:50Welcome to Rails World 2026: DHH on AI euphoria

AI euphoria, not AI psychosis

  • Opens in Austin; frames the moment as the most exciting thing computers have done in his career.
  • Acknowledges the unease: nobody knows the end state, and predictions go stale almost immediately.
“I prefer a different term. I have AI delirium. AI euphoria.”
▶ 4:00
021:50–4:15What portrait painters can teach us about AI

Portraits as 18th-century state of the art

  • Commissioned portraits took months of a master painter's time and were reserved for nobility and royalty (Reynolds' Ladies Waldegrave, Goya's royal family).
  • Anecdote: a Reynolds painting was rejected by the client over a visible ankle, so he redid it.
  • Painting technique improved only marginally over centuries.
▶ 5:48
034:15–6:38What portrait painters can teach us about AI

The Kodak Brownie changes the job

  • Photography arrives ~1840; Laurits Tuxen still spends three years on a Danish royal family portrait (1886).
  • 1900: Kodak's ~$1 Brownie democratizes photography.
  • Realist portrait skill stops being economically viable; painters pivot to new forms of art.
“The job was going to be different.”
▶ 8:46
046:38–9:01What portrait painters can teach us about AI

An explosion of creativity, and a family story

  • The shift drove Cubism (Picasso) and the impressionist Skagen painters.
  • Reveal: Laurits Tuxen is DHH's great-great-grandfather; the woman in pink is his great-grandmother.
  • Tuxen himself sat for a photograph late in life. Technology then stalled for decades; DHH's own childhood photos were few.
“It comes in starts and stops and fits.”
▶ 11:06
059:01–11:20What portrait painters can teach us about AI

From scarce snapshots to two trillion a year

  • Cameras from the 1920s (Leica I) to the 1980s were broadly similar; photos were still modest in number.
  • Digital and phone cameras made photos frictionless and "too cheap to measure".
  • ~2 trillion photos taken per year in 2026: same core technology, but past an inflection point. Parallel to software.
“It simply became too cheap to measure.”
▶ 11:32
0611:20–12:43November 24, 2025: the Kodak Brownie of our era

Nov 24, 2025: the Brownie of our era

  • Opus 4.5 is named as the tipping point: capable agentic coding, affordable and accessible.
  • "Everything before November 24th, and everything after."
  • Open-weight models with similar intelligence followed quickly.
“There was everything before November 24th. And then there was everything after.”
▶ 13:12
0712:43–16:02The trough of disillusionment, and the leap that followed

Trough of disillusionment, then the leap

  • Enjoyed Kimi K2.5 fast mode (~200 tok/s).
  • Feb-May 2026: new models felt like steps backward; markets wobbled, "it's over" takes.
  • June: Fable 5 and Mythos end the trough; agents go from "do this for me" to work he wants to merge.
  • GPT-6 Astra (Sept) and DeepSeek-4-1 Flash show frontier intelligence isn't a monopoly.
“This is where my diagnosis really set in.”
▶ 16:54
0816:02–18:13From the 10x programmer to the 1,000x programmer

10x → 100x → 1,000x programmer

  • The "10x programmer" idea traces to a 1968 study (5-30x variance); debated for ~45 years.
  • Claims 100x between the worst programmer without AI tools and the best with them is now uncontroversial.
  • Goes further: 1,000x. Asks what that means for companies and competition.
▶ 20:29
0918:13–20:45"Look at all the things I'm not doing": the Rails moment

"Look at all the things I'm not doing"

  • In the past 20 months he's written half as much code as in the previous 21 years.
  • Plays a clip from his 2005 Rails demo in Brazil celebrating code he didn't have to write.
  • Now: no hand-written code for ~5 months, yet every annoyance and wishlist feature is within reach.
“This is the Rails moment.”
▶ 22:03
1020:45–22:1237signals goes pencils down on hand-written code

37signals goes pencils down

  • 37signals has decided hand-writing code is no longer the normal course of business.
  • Hand-written code is now an exception, treated like a bug in Sentry: fix the agent, "fix the factory".
  • Polls the room: only about 5 people still write material code by hand weekly.
“Writing code by hand at 37signals is now an exceptional state.”
▶ 22:56
1122:12–24:04What vibe-coding Basecamp 5 taught us

Lessons from vibe-coding Basecamp 5

  • In spring, designers vibe-coded final Basecamp 5 features. Individually fine, collectively left the architecture "like Swiss cheese".
  • They retreated to manual review. In hindsight the wrong conclusion; newer models would have handled it.
  • The only serious question now: how do you get the most out of this intelligence explosion?
“There is only one serious question.”
▶ 24:23
1224:04–26:12Rebuilding HEY as native apps

HEY Next: no longer a web app

  • The next version of HEY drops the web app in favor of native apps.
  • HEY was a web app because that's what small teams could maintain; hence React Native, Hotwire Native, etc.
  • Six native apps kicked off about a week before the talk are already far along.
“Hey never really wanted to be a web app.”
▶ 26:31
1326:12–28:14Rebuilding HEY as native apps

Native everywhere, nearly free

  • "Not writing a line of code" but writing lots of prompts.
  • Many apps are web apps out of necessity or team size; with near-zero cost, those become native.
  • Shows a rough first Windows build, then a polished one 20 minutes later.
  • Cites Shopify's Shop app rewritten natively by a tiny team.
“The price of developing those things has gone to damn near zero.”
▶ 29:13
1428:14–30:42Rethinking HEY's backend with agents

The backend: Rust, as long as he never reads it

  • Calls Rust the ugliest language in decades, inhumane for humans to write.
  • But if agents write it and he never looks, he loves the outcome: 30-100x faster, tiny binaries, sub-ms startup.
  • A new division of labor: he specifies, agents write Rust.
“Rust is amazing if you never, ever, ever have to look at it yourself.”
▶ 31:39
1530:42–33:04Rethinking HEY's backend with agents

HEY's backend on a Raspberry Pi

  • Turning HEY into a Rust mail server: ~99% less CPU, ~95% less memory; 10 hosts only for redundancy.
  • Back-of-envelope: peak traffic could fit on a single Raspberry Pi.
  • Agents work best asynchronously, like delegating to a coworker, not in a chat window.
  • Outcome-level delegation is only months old; nobody knows the right workflow yet.
▶ 33:15
1633:04–34:23Where does this leave Ruby and Rails?

Where does this leave Ruby and Rails?

  • For HEY: native front ends + Rust back end.
  • The web still wins where users won't install anything; Rails remains well positioned there.
  • Convention over configuration maps to token efficiency; the "one-person framework" fits the agent era.
▶ 34:41
1734:23–36:28Agent evals with Evil Martians and the Rails Foundation

Agent evals with Evil Martians

  • Evil Martians run Rails agent evals for the Rails Foundation; v1 saturated at ~95% quickly, so it was made harder.
  • Warning to experts: don't be overly prescriptive. A beginner's mindset and higher-level prompts work better.
  • He treats Rust output as a black box, like any business owner who commissions software.
“I don't know any Rust at all. I consider that a feature.”
▶ 36:42
1836:28–38:06150,000 lines of code in a month

150,000 lines in a month

  • Ruby was 55% of his work over 21 years; this year ~3%.
  • Historic average: ~30k lines of production Ruby per year.
  • August 2026: ~150k lines in one month, ~60x his long-run average (verbose Rust inflates it, but the magnitude matters).
▶ 38:36
1938:06–39:21English: the programming language DHH likes better than Ruby

English > Ruby

  • Surprised to find a language he likes more than Ruby: English.
  • More expressive, if vaguer and less deterministic, and a joy to program in.
  • He got into programming for outcomes, fell in love with code, and now embraces outcomes again.
“English is a better programming language than Ruby.”
▶ 41:36
2039:21–42:49Retiring from hand-written code, with joy

Retired programmer → energized maker

  • Considers himself retired from professional programming since around March 2026.
  • Look back on 25 years of hand-chiseled code with joy, not regret, and accept it's over.
  • Claims hand-writing code is no longer economically productive for most programmers, and soon for nearly all.
  • The new career: a professional maker steering intelligence. Bigger than the arrival of the internet.
“Not with regret, but with joy of what was.”
▶ 43:12
2142:49–45:23Rethinking software architecture for the age of agents

Rethinking software architecture

  • Abstractions (and naming) were the main tool for keeping code mutable.
  • With many agents mutating a codebase, abstractions become choke points.
  • Repetition and keeping things in sync are now near-free, so DRY trade-offs shift.
  • Methodology too is open: cycle length, who specifies what. "You're at the ground floor."
“Abstractions don't make quite the same sense in the age of agents.”
▶ 45:47
2245:23–48:05Bring your own agent: why every app needs a CLI

Bring your own agent: ship a CLI

  • Rejects bolted-on in-app chatbots: users have their own agent ("butler").
  • The one prescriptive ask: every app should have a CLI. "By next Friday."
  • Example: the HEY CLI let an agent find a 5-year-old email by concept ("sneakers and a podcast") where Elasticsearch couldn't.
“Let me bring my own butler to the party.”
▶ 49:23
2348:05–51:21Omarchy: fixing the whole computer

Omarchy: fixing the whole computer

  • "We can fix everything" now applies to the whole OS: Omarchy.
  • ~$20M raised for the Omarchy effort.
  • Install time: 3m33s at last year's Rails World → 35s on an AMD laptop → 9s in the lab.
  • Quotes Mitchell Hashimoto: the pursuit of excellence needs no justification.
“The pursuit of excellence does not need justification.”
▶ 52:59
2451:21–53:53One-shot apps: a calculator, a writing app, a video editor, and Hype

One-shot apps

  • Calculator in C++/Qt, theme-matched to Omarchy: one-shot from a screenshot, shipped in a new ISO within minutes.
  • A personal iA Writer-style writing app; never read a line of its code.
  • A simple video trimmer, now included in Omarchy.
  • Hype: Markdown-based presentation software built while preparing this keynote.
“C++ as a black box is a great language.”
▶ 54:03
2553:53–55:02The performance payoff: half a megabyte

The performance payoff

  • Hype's binary is half a megabyte.
  • Two decades of hardware gains were spent on human productivity, yielding bloated apps (e.g. a 1.2 GB music player).
  • Now every optimization is within reach; agents can run overnight for 10-30x improvements.
“Half a megabyte.”
▶ 57:14
2655:02–58:26AI concerns, security, and why predictions fail

Concerns, security, and failed predictions

  • Concerns deserve airing; some, like security, are real: "something is coming, get ready."
  • Economic predictions at paradigm shifts are almost always wrong.
  • ATMs were expected to wipe out bank tellers; cheaper branches meant more branches and more tellers.
  • Truman vs. Oppenheimer: even the bomb's inventor couldn't predict what followed. Call for humility.
“Maybe we should also have a little humility about predictions of the future.”
▶ 58:47
2758:26–60:49P(bloom) over P(doom)

P(bloom) over P(doom)

  • Abundance is far more likely than doom.
  • Nuclear power: a side effect squandered for 40 years. Humanity can correct mistakes.
  • Security issues are solvable with the same intelligence; mentions a recent Rails CVE and an upcoming talk on HotCell quarantining.
  • Jevons' paradox: ~30k US bank tellers in 1950 → ~40k by ~2010.
“No one knows anything about the future.”
▶ 61:09
2860:49–63:07The case for total optimism

The case for total optimism

  • Game theory: given uncertainty, optimism is the only rational play.
  • "Agent Luther": a reformation of the computer that disintermediates the programmer "cleric class".
  • More competition is fine; Rails devs are "the best of the best".
  • Shows a child trying a kids' edition of Omarchy. The next generation has less to unlearn.
“Take the optimism pill.”
